title: Landlord Resolution Pipeline
heading: Landlord resolution pipeline
intro: How two HPD owner records become one landlord. Record work prepares the data, a Fellegi-Sunter model scores each candidate pair in bits, a gate with two vetoes protects precision, and a final pass joins offices that share a company. Select any box for what it does, the numbers for one real landlord (Domenico Antonelli), and what is measured or still open. From v0.2.0 a run can also return the decisions behind its clusters. The Release evidence tab on each box says what is recorded at that step and shows the rows that a beneficial-owner-resolution release stores for it, with the names and addresses they stand for.

views.label: Pipeline
views.title: Pipeline overview
views.desc: HPD owner contacts are extracted into records, hub addresses are masked, candidate pairs are blocked on surname and first initial, scored, gated by a threshold and two vetoes into base groups, then joined further by a shared-company pass. The result is a set of owner entities. Whole-city statistics feed three stages.

input.title: HPD owner contacts
input.lede: The only data the engine needs: who is named as an owner on each building's HPD registration, and the business address they gave.
what: Four owner roles count: HeadOfficer, IndividualOwner, CorporateOwner and JointOwner. Agents and site managers are not owners, because they are shared across unrelated landlords.
Only the most recent registration for each building (BBL) is used.
The same SQL runs on Postgres or on an offline DuckDB snapshot.
nums: person-owner records in the September 2026 data
open: A registration says who filed, not who owns the building today. Three of Antonelli's ten buildings were sold in 2024 by his estate, and the registrations still list him.

evidence.lede: A resolution that captures its decisions remembers which HPD contact records each identity stands on. That link is what lets a later reader go from a decision back to the registrations.
recorded: For every identity, the registration and contact ids of the rows it was built from (the sources column).
In the release these are observations, written registration:contact:k, never a name.
tables: Which observation stands behind which identity and building (199,405 rows).

examples.caption: One of Antonelli's records stands on two contact records, two buildings.
examples.note: Domenico Antonelli's nine records are I0009556 and eight other identities; identity_names gives each its name and address.

examples.caption: Two of his contact records, and who they name. Join them to HPD on registration and contact id.

limits: A contact record says who filed a registration, not who owns the building. The release records the filing, not the ownership.

stats.title: City-wide statistics
stats.lede: Three counts taken over every record, so a rare name or a hub is judged against the whole city and not against a sample.
what: Name rarity: the number of distinct identities that share a surname and first initial. The common-name veto starts above 15.
Address degree: the number of distinct landlords registered at one house number and street. Above 25, the address is treated as an aggregator.
Company degree: the number of distinct named contacts listed under a company name. Above 25, the second pass ignores that company.
open: The cutoffs are fixed constants, not learned. Company degree counts named contacts under a company name, not clients, so it is only a rough filter.

evidence.lede: The city-wide counts are not stored. The cutoffs applied to them are, so a reader knows which rule was in force.
recorded: The three cutoffs: address degree 25, name rarity 15 and company degree 25.
The model threshold, seed and first-name similarity.
For each record that was masked, the address degree that triggered it.

examples.caption: The resolution parameters of the run.

limits: The counts themselves (name frequencies, address degrees) are not in the release, only their effect on decisions.

s1.title: 1 · Extract
s1.lede: Turns raw contact rows into one record per distinct name and business address, with the buildings that record registers.
what: The grain is (kind, name, raw business address). A person who files from three addresses becomes three records. That fragmentation is what resolution repairs.

It prepares the matching fields: a normalized name with LLC or INC suffixes removed, the street without its suffix (WEST 21ST STREET becomes WEST 21ST), first initial, apartment number and ZIP. Missing values stay null, so a comparison is skipped instead of matched.
Each record gets a deterministic id (an md5 of its identity), so reruns line up.
Only person records are resolved. Organizations and LLCs pass through unresolved.
nums: WoW portfolios those buildings sit in
open: A typo creates a new record (POWELLS COW B). The later stages exist to reunite exactly these.

evidence.lede: Each record the extract builds is an identity. The release says which contact records it stands on and which cluster it ended in.
recorded: An opaque identity id for every record (145,388), local to the run, and the name and business address that define it.
The buildings and contact records each identity covers.
Its base cluster after the gate and its final cluster after the shared-company pass.
tables: The name and business address of each identity (145,412 rows, 24 of them removed by a curated list).
identity to contact record and building.

examples.caption: Antonelli's nine records: one name, nine addresses, five base clusters and one final cluster.
examples.note: Domenico Antonelli's nine records are I0009556 and eight other identities; identity_names gives each its name and address.

limits: The name and address are copied as filed. A typo makes a new record (POWELLS COW B), which is what the later stages reunite.
The identity id is not stable across runs.

s2.title: 2 · Mask hub addresses
s2.lede: Blanks the address evidence at any address shared by many landlords, so office-mates are not fused.
what: A house number and street used by more than 25 distinct landlords (a registered agent, an office suite, a law firm) has its address fields cleared before scoring.
Name evidence still counts. Without the address, two different people at one hub stop looking alike.
Degrees are computed over the whole city, so a hub is a hub wherever the sample falls.
nums: landlords at one address means a hub
open: The address is matched as a string. The same hub written two ways splits into two smaller addresses, and either can slip under the cutoff.

evidence.lede: Masking leaves one event per record whose address evidence was blanked, with the degree that caused it.
recorded: The record, the rule and the address degree.
The outcome masked, with the reason address_evidence_masked.
tables: 5,298 masked records in this run (stage identity.splink_base).

examples.caption: Three records whose address evidence was blanked.

limits: The event records the degree and the identity. The record's address is in identity_names, so a reader can see which hub it was.

s3.title: 3 · Block
s3.lede: Only records that share a surname and a first initial are ever compared.
what: There is one blocking rule: same last name and same first initial. It is the entry ticket to scoring and is never enough on its own.
An address-only rule was removed. At city scale it fused 2,044 clusters of different people who share an office, with different surnames and the same first initial.
The cost: a typo in the surname means the pair is never a candidate.
open: Surname typos are not recovered. The code notes a typo-safe block could be added later.

evidence.lede: Blocking is not recorded. A pair that was never compared leaves no row.
recorded: Nothing. Only pairs that reach the gate are kept, so a pair blocked out here is invisible in the release.
limits: Absence of an event means the rule did not run. It never means the records were found to differ.

s4.title: 4 · Score
s4.lede: Each candidate pair gets a match weight in bits: the evidence that the records are one person, added to a steep negative prior.
what: Five comparisons: surname and first name (fuzzy, with a term-frequency adjustment so a rare name counts for more), business house number, street, and ZIP.
Match weight is the prior (about −18 bits) plus the evidence from each comparison. Turn the weight back into odds to get the probability.
The weights are learned on a dense slice of the data (every record that shares a surname and initial with another) and applied to the whole city, so a few common names do not bend the prior.
Pairs below 0.5 are dropped.
nums: bits: Antonelli's name evidence, 6.1 of it from term frequency
open: The street comparison measures string similarity, so numbered streets look alike (147TH and 154TH).
Probabilities shift slightly between training runs.

evidence.lede: The score is stored as a probability, with the threshold it was held against, only for pairs at or above the threshold.
recorded: The match probability of each pair above 0.999 and the threshold.
Pairs below the threshold are not stored.
tables: score and threshold on each pair event (stage identity.splink_base).

examples.caption: Two of Antonelli's pairs that cleared 0.999 by a small margin, and the addresses compared.
examples.note: The model's probability, not its bits. A probability of 0.999 is about 10 bits of match weight.

limits: The probability of a pair is the model's, not the chance a whole cluster is right.
The model's bits and the term-frequency parts of a score are not stored.

s5.title: 5 · Gate
s5.lede: A pair becomes a link only when its probability is at least 0.999 and neither veto objects.
what: 0.999 is a match weight of about 10 bits.
First-name veto: if the first names genuinely disagree (JACOB and JOSEF), the link is dropped, even with a strong address match.
Common-name veto: a name shared by more than 15 identities is not linked on name alone when the addresses differ (two unrelated JIN CHENs).
The surviving links form groups. Groups are connected components, so joins chain.
nums: base groups for Antonelli, down from 9 portfolios
measured: In the labeled sample, all 49 links that join separate WoW portfolios through this stage were correct (interval 93 to 100%).
open: The threshold is a bright line through evidence of uneven quality. One Antonelli pair clears it by 0.6 bits and another misses by 2.7.

evidence.lede: Every pair above the threshold gets a decision: accepted, or rejected by a named veto.
recorded: Accepted pairs, with the cluster they joined.
Rejected pairs, with first_name_veto or common_name_veto. A common-name veto also records the name rarity and whether the addresses matched.
The base clusters that result, as base_cluster_id on each identity.
tables: base_cluster_id: the groups after this stage.

examples.caption: Two of Antonelli's pairs, accepted and put in the same cluster: the same name at two spellings and two addresses.
The first-name veto: JOSEF and JACOB at one address, above 0.999 and refused.
The common-name veto: 73 look-alike names, and addresses that differ.

limits: A pair below the threshold is not recorded, so a veto event shows only the pairs that would otherwise have joined.

s6.title: 6 · Shared-company pass
s6.lede: Joins groups that share a rare name and a company named on their registrations. It connects offices at unrelated addresses.
what: Two groups merge when all of these hold: the same surname and first initial; compatible first names (STEVE and STEVEN pass, JACOB and JOSEF do not); a rare name (at most 15 identities); and a company name that appears on both groups' registrations.
The company can be an owner or the managing agent. The pass does not tell them apart.
A company listed under more than 25 named contacts is ignored.
For Antonelli, Carollo Management, the HPD agent, joins his five office groups into one.
nums: of re-linked buildings exist only because of it
measured: Sampled links through this pass: 15 of 18 correct (interval 61 to 94%), against 49 of 49 for name and address. The split was made after the errors were seen, so read it as a lead.
open: All three errors were different people with the same full name, bridged only by a management company, each with a WoW portfolio of 50+ buildings on one side.
A shared manager is evidence of management, not ownership. Where the shared company also appears as an owner of record, all 6 sampled links were right.
Open question: ship it as its own edge type, or leave it out of a first patch.

evidence.lede: The shared-company pass logs each pair of groups it considered. Accepted merges and refusals both leave events, and the contact records that carry the company are attached.
recorded: For each pair of base clusters: accepted, or refused with the reason.
The number of shared companies, and the contact records that carry them.
Refusal reasons: name not rare, first name conflict, company degree over the cap, or company degree unknown.
tables: 1,197 accepted; 830 refused (371 name not rare, 209 degree unknown, 175 first-name conflict, 75 degree cap).
17,310 rows: the contact records behind these events, role shared_company. observation_contacts says who each is.

examples.caption: Four of the ten merges that join Antonelli's five base clusters into one.
examples.note: Ten pairs for five groups: one shared company links every group to every other.

examples.caption: The contacts that carry the shared company: three of Antonelli's registrations list the same managing agent.
A refusal elsewhere: the surnames and initials match and a company is shared, but the first names conflict.
Some of the 17 contact records that carry that company.

limits: Management evidence stands in for ownership here. The company is the managing agent's, not necessarily the owner's.
Only pairs with a shared company are logged. Others leave no row.

outcome.title: Owner entities
outcome.lede: Each final group becomes an owner id. The patch adds a splink edge between the graph nodes in the same group.
what: owner_index maps (normalized name, building) to an owner id. Ids are stable within one run only.
The WoW patch adds one edge type (splink, weight 10) between nodes that resolve to the same owner. WoW's connected-components and Louvain steps run unchanged on the larger graph.
Edges only add, so connected components can only merge.
nums: sampled links judged the same owner
of those that join separate WoW portfolios
open: Precision only. Recall is not estimated, and the absence of a link does not mean two owners differ.
Labels are one human annotator's. A blind second reader is planned, and the figures are provisional until then.

evidence.lede: The result is a set of clusters. In the release, a cluster is the final answer for identities, and the events explain it.
recorded: Every identity, its base cluster and its final cluster.

The question is whether they are the same person. If they are, their buildings belong to one owner entity.

v-block.title: Same surname + first initial?
v-block.lede: Records that differ in surname or first initial are never scored against each other.
what: No: the pair is never compared, so no link can form between them.
Yes: the pair goes on to scoring.
open: A typo in the surname removes the pair from consideration.

evidence.lede: Blocking leaves no record.
recorded: Nothing. A pair that is never compared has no event.
limits: An absent event means the rule did not run.

v-notcomp.title: Not compared
v-notcomp.lede: The records share no surname and first initial, so the engine says nothing about them.
what: This is not a finding that the owners differ. It is the absence of any comparison.

evidence.lede: There is no row for a pair that was not compared.
recorded: Nothing.
limits: Not compared is not a finding that the owners differ.

v-score.title: Match weight above about 10 bits?
v-score.lede: The weight sums name and address evidence on top of a prior of about −18 bits. About 10 bits is a probability of 0.999.
what: Antonelli's pair D–E (147TH STREET and 154TH STREET, same ZIP) reaches 10.6 bits and passes.
Pair E–G reaches 7.3 bits and falls short. Pair D–F reaches 5.1 bits.
Pairs that fall short are not rejected outright. They go on to the shared-company test.
open: Select the Score box on the Pipeline tab to see these pairs as waterfall charts.

evidence.lede: A pair that clears the score is recorded with its probability and the threshold.
recorded: Probability, threshold and outcome.

examples.caption: D–E: the 154TH STREET and 147TH STREET records, accepted.

limits: Pairs that fall short are not recorded. They still go on to the shared-company test.

v-first.title: First names agree?
v-first.lede: A link is dropped when both first names are present and genuinely disagree.
what: Genuine disagreement means Jaro-Winkler similarity below 0.80. JACOB and JOSEF fail. STEVE and STEVEN, and ZACH and ZACHARY, pass.
A missing first name passes.
Nicknames that are not near-matches (ABE and ABRAHAM) fail too. That is a deliberate precision trade.

evidence.lede: A first-name veto is an event with the reason first_name_veto.
recorded: The pair, its probability and the reason.

examples.caption: JOSEF and JACOB: refused although they score above 0.999.

limits: The first names are in identity_names. The veto compares them by similarity, not equality.

v-common.title: Common name at different addresses?
v-common.lede: A name that many people share is not enough to link records at different addresses.
what: A name is common when more than 15 identities share its surname and first initial.
Addresses are compared after normalizing house digits and street suffix, so 140-06 and 14006 count as the same address.
Yes: the link is dropped. No: the pair joins on name and address.
nums: identities share ANTONELLI + D, so it is rare

evidence.lede: A common-name veto is an event that also records the name rarity and whether the addresses matched.
recorded: The pair, its probability, the reason, and detail with name_rarity and same_address.

examples.caption: A pair of 73 look-alike names at different addresses.

limits: The name rarity is a count of identities sharing a surname and first initial, taken over the whole city.

v-second.title: Shared-company test
v-second.lede: Pairs that did not join on name and address get one more chance, through a company they share.
what: The name must be rare, the first names compatible, and the groups' buildings must share a company named on their registrations (an owner or a managing agent). Companies listed under more than 25 named contacts are ignored.
A common name can never pass this test, so a pair stopped by the common-name veto stays separate.
The decision is really made between groups, not single pairs, so one shared company can join several offices at once.
measured: Sampled links through this test: 15 of 18 correct.
open: Management evidence stands in for ownership evidence here. See stage 6 on the Pipeline tab.

evidence.lede: The shared-company test is logged for every pair of groups with a shared company, whether it passes or not.
recorded: Accepted or refused, the reason, and the contact records that carry the company.

examples.caption: Refusal for a conflict of first names, and the first merge that joined Antonelli's groups.

limits: The release shows which contacts carry the company (decision_support) and who they are (observation_contacts), not a single company name per event.

v-join-a.title: JOIN on name and address
v-join-a.lede: The records score high enough, the first names agree, and the name is not common at different addresses.
what: The strongest evidence the engine has: a rare name together with matching or near-matching address fields.
Example: Powells Cove Boulevard and Powells Cow B join at 26 bits.
nums: sampled links through this route that join separate WoW portfolios were correct

evidence.lede: A join on name and address is an accepted pair event that names the cluster.
recorded: The pair, its probability and cluster_id.

examples.caption: An accepted pair.

limits: 97% of 150 sampled links in this stratum were judged the same owner, on a provisional gold.

v-join-b.title: JOIN on a shared company
v-join-b.lede: The records share a rare name and a company on their registrations, though their addresses do not match.
what: This is how Antonelli's offices at unrelated addresses become one entity, through Carollo Management.
nums: sampled links through this route were correct
open: The three errors in the sample came through this route.

v-sep.title: Stays separate
v-sep.lede: No route produced a link, so the engine makes no claim about these records.
what: This is not a finding that the owners differ. Recall is not estimated, and the absence of a link does not mean two owners are different.

evidence.lede: Records that stay separate leave a row only when a rule refused them.

v-entity.title: Owner entity
v-entity.lede: Joins chain. Records linked directly or through other records form one owner entity.
what: If A joins B and B joins C, all three are one entity even when A and C would not join on their own.
Each entity becomes an owner id, and the patch adds edges between its nodes in WoW's graph.
open: Chaining means one wrong link can merge two whole groups.

evidence.lede: An owner entity is a cluster id, with the identities that belong to it.
recorded: Identity to cluster.

examples.caption: Antonelli's cluster, with each record's address.

limits: Chaining means one wrong link can merge two whole groups. The events show which links did it.
